title: Your own notebook
hook: Marcus wrote to himself, and so can you

segments.voice: Yesterday: what Marcus kept returning to, death, the whole, duty, kindness, the present. Your line was my theme. Which one did you write down? Day six hundred thirty-nine.

Notes app, a voice memo, the back of a receipt. Most of us already write to ourselves: grocery lists, reminders, half a thought at 2am. Almost none of it is meant for anyone else, and almost all of it gets deleted. Marcus Aurelius did the same thing, in Greek, in army camps on the frontier. He didn't write for us. He wrote to himself, the way you'd leave a note on the fridge. And it survived. Today: your own notebook.
screen: `NOTES APP, VOICE MEMO, A RECEIPT.` → `GREEK, IN AN ARMY CAMP, AT NIGHT.` → `YOUR OWN NOTEBOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the title. In the old manuscripts the book is called Ta eis heauton: the things to himself. Scholars doubt Marcus gave it that name, but it fits. Meditations is a later English title. Second, the place. Two of the books carry little headings: one written among the Quadi, by the river Granua; another at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube. So at least some of it was written on campaign, by a tired man around fifty, at war on the frontier. Not in a library. Third, how he talks. Read any page and notice the voice: you. You'll meet difficult people today. You're getting angry again. Remember. He isn't explaining Stoicism to a reader. He's coaching the one person who most needs it, and he's honest with him. He repeats himself. He scolds himself. He changes his mind. That's what a notebook is for. Fourth, why it works. Writing a rule down is different from knowing it. The pen slows you down. It makes the vague thing exact. And rereading your own words, later, in your own handwriting, lands differently from reading anyone else's. Marcus wasn't writing a classic. He was practicing, the way a musician practices scales, and the practice happened to be on paper. Nothing stops anyone from doing the same. No Greek, no empire, no audience required. Three honest lines, to yourself, are already a notebook.
screen: `TA EIS HEAUTON: TO HIMSELF.` · `WRITTEN ON CAMPAIGN BY A RIVER.` · `THE VOICE IS "YOU."` · `THE PEN MAKES IT EXACT.` · then, large: `TO MYSELF.`

segments.voice: If you can, get something to write with: paper, or the notes on your phone. Breathe once or twice. Now write three lines to yourself, the way Marcus did, using you. One line about something you keep forgetting. One about a person you'll see today. One about what matters most this week. Don't make them pretty. Make them true. Then read them back once, slowly, as if someone who loves you wrote them. The bell holds the time.
Your own notebook. Marcus wrote the Meditations to himself, on campaign, for no reader but one. Anyone can keep the same kind of notebook. Today's word.
Your line: to myself. Before you sleep, reread your three lines, and add one more, about what today taught you. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Many people who read Marcus keep a private notebook of their own, writing short reminders to themselves in the second person and rereading them.

fork.setup: you want to keep a notebook like Marcus's. what do you write first?
options: a polished essay for others to read.
three honest lines to yourself, using "you."
fork.reveal: Marcus coached himself in plain second-person reminders. no audience, no polish, just practice on paper.

original.note: Greek: the things to himself. The title found in the manuscripts of the Meditations.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Meditations are a philosophy book.
what it means: a private notebook, written to himself, partly on campaign, that happened to survive.
what a scholar hears: the title Ta eis heauton appears in the manuscripts but probably isn't Marcus's own, and the headings to books two and three place the writing among the Quadi and at Carnuntum.

notes: The headings 'among the Quadi at the Granua' and 'at Carnuntum' stand at the end of book 1 / start of book 2 and at the start of book 3 in the manuscripts; editors differ on placement. Phrased as 'two of the books carry little headings'; confirm.
Title Τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν: transmitted in the manuscript tradition; most scholars doubt it is Marcus's own. Confirm.
Marcus was around fifty at Carnuntum (born 121; based there c. 171–173; wars c. 166–180). Confirm.
